clinical_knowledge.topic: Severe Symptomatic Pectus Excavatum evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Severe Symptomatic Pectus Excavatum is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Refer to cardiothoracic/pediatric surgery for Minimally Invasive Repair of Pectus Excavatum (MIRPE - Nuss procedure) involving substernal placement of a curved titanium bar under thoracoscopic guidance to elevate the sternum, or open Ravitch procedure, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: severe concave depression of breastbone causing exercise shortness of breath and body image distress

Key HPI features: 19F college swimmer presents for evaluation of a deep, bowl-shaped sternal depression present since early childhood that rapidly deepened during adolescent growth spurt. Complains of decreased exercise tolerance, feeling out of breath during competitive swim heats, and palpitations. Reports severe psychological distress and embarrassment regarding anterior chest wall deformity.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 68, BP 114/70. Anterior chest wall examination reveals a deep lower sternal and costal cartilage posterior depression with leftward displacement of the cardiac apex impulse. Non-contrast chest CT demonstrates severe pectus excavatum with a Haller Index of 4.8 (normal < 2.5; severe indication for surgery > 3.25), causing direct anterior compression of the right ventricle during diastole. Echocardiogram shows mild mitral valve prolapse and right ventricular outflow tract dynamic narrowing during exercise.
Relevant background/PMH: No other chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Severe Symptomatic Pectus Excavatum.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Pectus carinatum (opposite deformity) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Palpitations with exertion — suggests cardiac compression significant enough to affect rhythm.
management_principles: Refer to cardiothoracic/pediatric surgery for Minimally Invasive Repair of Pectus Excavatum (MIRPE - Nuss procedure) involving substernal placement of a curved titanium bar under thoracoscopic guidance to elevate the sternum, or open Ravitch procedure
Pre-operative physical therapy and pain management protocol counseling (cryoablation of intercostal nerves during surgery to minimize post-op pain)
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

learning_objectives: Calculate and interpret the Haller Index from chest CT (transverse diameter divided by AP sternovertebral distance; severe > 3.25)
Correlate right ventricular diastolic compression and reduced cardiac output with exercise intolerance in severe pectus excavatum
Compare surgical correction techniques: Minimally Invasive Nuss Procedure (substernal bar placement) vs Open Ravitch Procedure (cartilage resection and sternal osteotomy)
Understand multidisciplinary perioperative pain management including intercostal nerve cryoablation and epidural analgesia

teaching.one_liner: A congenital, progressively deepening depression of the sternum that can compress the heart and reduce exercise capacity — corrected with the minimally invasive Nuss procedure.
red_flags: Palpitations with exertion — suggests cardiac compression significant enough to affect rhythm

history.answer: My chest bone has been sunken in for years, and lately it's making me really short of breath when I swim fast.
I've had a slight dip in the middle of my chest since I was a little girl, but it deepened a lot during middle and high school when I had my growth spurt.
It's right in the center of my lower breastbone, forming a deep bowl shape between my ribs.
It's quite deep and hollow, deep enough that a fist could almost fit in it, and it feels completely solid and bony.
At rest I breathe completely fine, but whenever I push hard during swim practice or compete in sprint heats, I get winded way faster than my teammates.
Yes, during or right after intense swim sets, my heart suddenly feels like it's fluttering or racing in my chest.
I don't get sharp or crushing chest pain, just a feeling of pressure and tightness when I breathe heavily during exercise.
I have felt slightly lightheaded after an all-out swim sprint, but I've never passed out or blacked out.
No, I don't have any cough, wheezing, or asthma symptoms.
Resting and catching my breath helps, while hard exertion, especially freestyle sprinting, brings on the breathing trouble right away.
No fever, chills, night sweats, or unexpected weight loss at all.
A pediatrician looked at it when I was around twelve and told us it was a sunken chest, but we never had formal scans or specialist visits done back then.
I tried posture exercises and back-strengthening workouts in high school, but they didn't change the shape of the bone at all.
It has been very hard emotionally, and I avoid wearing fitted clothes or regular swimsuits outside of swim practice because I feel so self-conscious.
I worry that as I get older it might press even harder on my heart and cause permanent damage, or keep me from continuing competitive swimming.
I honestly feel like the sunken bone is physically squishing my lungs and heart, keeping them from expanding when I breathe hard.
I would really like to know if surgery can fix the dent in my chest, expand my lung capacity, and make my chest look normal.
No, I don't have unusually stretchy skin, loose joints, or eye problems.
I don't have any other chronic medical conditions like high blood pressure, diabetes, or lung disease.
I have never had any surgeries and have never stayed overnight in a hospital.
I don't take any prescription medicines, over-the-counter drugs, or daily supplements.
I don't have any known allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used vape products.
I might have a single glass of wine on special social occasions, but usually I don't drink alcohol because of training.
I'm a sophomore in college studying biology, living in a campus dorm, and I swim competitively for the university team.
My periods are regular every twenty-eight days, and my last period started about two weeks ago.
I'm not sexually active right now, so there's no chance of pregnancy.
Nobody in my family has a sunken chest, Marfan syndrome, or early unexplained heart disease.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 114/70 mmHg, heart rate 68 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 99% on room air, and temperature 36.7°C.
Athletic, slender young female sitting comfortably in no acute distress at rest.
Marked symmetrical concave depression of the lower sternum and adjacent costal cartilages without chest wall tenderness, with the apical impulse visibly displaced to the left.
Resonant to percussion across all lung fields bilaterally.
Vesicular breath sounds clear bilaterally with good air entry and no wheezes, crackles, or rubs.
Normal S1 and S2 with a late systolic click audible at the left-shifted cardiac apex, regular rate and rhythm, and no murmur or gallop.
Straight thoracic spine without visible scoliosis or kyphoscoliotic deformity, with full pain-free range of motion.
Normal joint mobility without hyperextensibility, arachnodactyly, or swelling in the fingers, wrists, or knees.
Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light with normal extraocular movements and no gross lens dislocation.
Warm well-perfused extremities with strong bilateral radial and pedal pulses and no peripheral edema.
